ground_truth.title: What's Next in Climate Tech? Here are 5 Trends Experts Say You Can't Ignore
ground_truth.author: Nina Benoit
ground_truth.main_content:
Key insights into the trends driving the next wave of climate innovation

In this week’s newsletter, we had the privilege of speaking with leaders across sustainability, sustainable investing, and climate technology to gain insight into the key trends shaping the future of climate tech. These voices represent a cross-section of founders, investors, and innovators working to scale the solutions our planet needs.

As the world grapples with climate instability, increasing regulatory pressure, and the economic imperative to decarbonize, climate tech is emerging as one of the most dynamic sectors of the global economy. From clean energy to artificial intelligence, ocean-based innovation to policy-driven adaptation, the landscape is evolving fast and reshaping how we think about sustainability, business, and innovation.

1. Global Policy Is Driving Climate Tech Innovation

One of the clearest catalysts for climate tech advancement is national policy. Around the world, governments are setting ambitious emissions targets, introducing green building mandates, and offering incentives to accelerate decarbonization efforts.

Regions like Germany and the Netherlands are leading the way, where public infrastructure investments are actively fostering a supportive environment for climate innovation. Similarly, countries like Australia, Singapore, Hong Kong, and Japan are taking meaningful steps through legislation and funding to stimulate sustainable development.

“In essence, I would say that in markets such as Germany and the Netherlands—where governments are coupling large-scale investment in energy grids, critical infrastructure and digitisation with a clear push for innovation—we see a policy-driven foundation that is set to further accelerate growth and momentum across the broader energy/ infrastructure sector.” - Jan Fredriks, Managing Partner AIXTerra Ventures

These regulatory signals are creating fertile ground for climate tech entrepreneurs. However, they’re also introducing complexity, especially in regions where policies change frequently or where ESG frameworks are still evolving. In these markets, companies must remain agile, informed, and capable of aligning their technology with local compliance requirements.

2. The Convergence of Software and Consulting

As the climate tech sector matures, it’s becoming increasingly clear that delivering technology alone isn't enough. Many companies, particularly in ESG reporting, emissions tracking, and sustainability planning, are finding that software must be paired with strategic consulting to be effective.

Organizations navigating climate disclosure regulations or carbon accounting standards often lack the internal expertise to interpret and act on new policies. As a result, climate tech platforms that combine user-friendly tools with advisory support are gaining a competitive edge. Whether it’s helping clients comply with CSRD, CDP, the ASRS, California’s SB219, or Science Based Targets, value is being created at the intersection of tech and tailored insight.

This hybrid model is not only helping clients keep up, it is also building trust and creating new revenue streams for providers who can deliver both the tools and the thinking behind them.

“I think this is a space where if you have an advisory arm, a little bit of consulting can be really helpful. Because I can see how many existing decision makers are not well-versed in ESG, and now there's these new policies that seem to change and update very frequently. They just don't have the time or energy to keep up with it.” - Chialin Yu, Strategy and Finance at Canary Technology

3. ROI Is the New North Star

Climate tech startups are increasingly facing a more rigorous funding environment due to market saturation and global governance trends. Investors today are looking beyond mission statements and policy tailwinds. They want clear evidence of market demand, healthy unit economics, and the ability to scale profitably.

The climate impact is important, but it’s no longer enough on its own. Startups need to win on price, performance, and user experience. This is especially true in categories where the customer’s willingness to pay is still evolving.

“Today, investors are asking whether there’s real demand and whether unit economics work. Startups relying heavily on regulation (e.g., circularity, ESG tools) have struggled. The bar is higher now: you need to win on price, performance, and customer experience, and the climate impact is the bonus, not the lead.” - Austin Wood, Investment Manager at SET Ventures

The silver lining? For the best companies, this environment is accelerating maturity. Climate tech solutions that can deliver cost savings, operational efficiency, and regulatory compliance are proving their value in ways that make them resilient to market cycles.

4. AI’s Role in Scaling Climate Solutions

Artificial intelligence is transforming nearly every industry, and climate tech is no exception. From predictive maintenance for renewable energy systems to optimizing supply chains for lower emissions, AI is driving smarter, faster, and more effective climate action.

The key challenge now is harnessing AI in ways that are both impactful and sustainable. Training large language models and running complex simulations requires significant energy. But when deployed thoughtfully, AI can amplify climate solutions rather than contradicting them.

AI’s potential in the climate space is massive: automating emissions tracking, simulating climate scenarios, optimizing building energy use, or improving climate risk modeling. As AI technologies become more accessible, they’re unlocking new capabilities across the climate innovation stack.

“AI's real value in climate work is time. It takes on the repetitive tasks that drain sustainability teams’ resources, such as data analysis, emissions tracking, and sustainability reporting, so they can focus on deeper thinking and strategic decisions. Its strength isn’t just in automation, but in revealing patterns and complexities that would otherwise take weeks or months to uncover.” - Chris Bolman, Co-Founder and CEO of Brightest

5. The Rise of the Blue Economy

While much of the climate tech conversation has historically focused on land-based innovation, oceans are taking center stage. The “Blue Economy”, a term encompassing sustainable ocean-based industries, is emerging as a new frontier for investment and innovation.

"2025 is the year for the blue economy which covers a wide spectrum of categories from technologies and biomaterials to replace and reduce plastic to data and AI solutions to help assess and monitor our ocean. The Blue Economy Finance Forum hosted by Monaco during the United Nations Ocean Conference this year was attended by investors from around the world and I've seen a huge wave of interest and capital moving into ocean-related start-ups. When it comes to the ocean, the scale and impact are unparalleled and the opportunity for returns and value to the planet are unprecedented." - Michelle Li, Founder & CEO of Clever Carbon

This includes a wide range of technologies: from seaweed-based biomaterials that replace plastic, to ocean carbon removal solutions, to satellite and AI systems that monitor marine ecosystems. The ocean offers incredible potential for carbon sequestration, biodiversity preservation, and climate resilience.

Global interest in the Blue Economy is accelerating. High-profile gatherings like the Blue Economy Finance Forum, hosted during the United Nations Ocean Conference in Monaco, are drawing attention from investors and startups alike. The convergence of capital, policy focus, and scientific urgency is fueling a wave of innovation that could redefine how we engage with the world’s oceans.

A Defining Decade for Climate Tech

The insights shared by our contributors this week paint a clear picture: climate tech is no longer niche. It is becoming central to how we build a better future. From regulatory shifts to market expectations, from AI to ocean innovation, the pace of change is accelerating, and the stakes have never been higher.

Thank you again to all of our participants who shared their perspectives, insights, and expertise. The road ahead will be challenging but also full of opportunity. As the climate and sustainability landscape continues to evolve, staying informed and adaptable will be key to driving meaningful progress. At Brightest, we’re committed to helping our community navigate it with clarity, and purpose.
